passage:
Pallavi: Met the new client today. Suit, gold watch, sunglasses on his head. Total show-off 😅
Uday: lol why
Pallavi: Who wears that to a warehouse meeting
Uday: Did he say something rude?
Pallavi: No... he actually asked the loaders their names
Uday: Hmm
Pallavi: He said the watch was his father's and he wears it for luck. And the suit is because it's his first big meeting
Uday: So you judged the watch before you asked
Pallavi: Fair. I assumed money and attitude
Uday: Ask next time, "nice watch, is there a story?" 🙂
Pallavi: Good line. Feeling a bit silly now

qa.q: Whose watch did the client say it was?
qa.a: His father's.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling at the end of the chat?
qa.a: A bit silly, having realised the guesses came from the client's look alone.

qa.q: What could Pallavi ask next time?
qa.a: Something like "nice watch, is there a story?"

qa.q: How might the client have felt if Pallavi had voiced the first guess?
qa.a: Judged or unwelcome, especially at his first big meeting.

grounding: A person guesses wealth and attitude from clothes and accessories, the guess is wrong, and respectful curiosity is the better response.

passage: At the small-town bus stand, Anand watched a woman step off the bus in jeans and a short haircut, carrying a steel toolbox. "City girl, lost," he thought, and offered to point her to the taxi stand. "Thanks, but I'm here for the Patil farm," Disha said. "Their buffalo has a hoof problem." Anand blinked. She was the new veterinary officer, and she had grown up two villages away. He felt his face burn. "Sorry, I assumed," he said. Disha smiled, half tired, half amused. "I get that often. Which way is the Patil farm?" Anand walked her there, asked about her work on the way, and listened.

qa.q: What was Disha carrying?
qa.a: A steel toolbox.

qa.q: What did Anand feel when he learned who Disha was?
qa.a: He was embarrassed, since his face burned, because his guess from her clothes and hair was wrong.

qa.q: What could Anand do differently next time?
qa.a: He can ask an open, respectful question first, like whether he can help her find something, without deciding who she is.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt about being mistaken for a lost city girl?
qa.a: Tired and amused, as she says it happens often, though it may also be wearing.

grounding: A person guesses a stranger's background from clothes and hair, is wrong, and moves to respectful curiosity.

passage: On her first day at the Johannesburg accounting firm, Amara noticed Zanele immediately: the sleek leather bag, the perfect nails, the heels that clicked across the lobby. Rich, Amara decided. Probably from a wealthy suburb, probably not interested in a new girl from Lagos. For a week she kept her distance, answering Zanele's hellos with a polite nod. Then, at the lunch table, Zanele caught her looking at the bag. Amara, embarrassed, said the first honest thing she could. "It's beautiful. I've been curious where it's from." Zanele laughed and turned it over to show the stitching. "My mother made it. She sews in Soweto, at the kitchen table. I take two taxis to get here every morning, and I do my nails myself on Sundays." Amara felt her cheeks heat. She'd built a whole person out of a bag. "I'm sorry. I think I judged you before I met you." Zanele shrugged, smiling. "Everyone does. Want to see her other bags?"

qa.q: Who made Zanele's bag?
qa.a: Her mother, who sews in Soweto.

qa.q: How did Amara feel when Zanele explained the bag?
qa.a: Amara felt embarrassed, cheeks heating, realising she had built a whole person out of a bag.

qa.q: What turned Amara's assumption around?
qa.a: Asking with honest, respectful curiosity where the bag was from, instead of keeping her distance based on a guess.

qa.q: How might Zanele have felt during that first week?
qa.a: Zanele may have felt puzzled or a little shut out, getting only polite nods to her hellos, though she seemed used to being judged.

grounding: Shows a young professional guessing a colleague's wealth and attitude from her clothes, being wrong, and respectful curiosity correcting it.

passage: At the university admissions office on the first day of term, the queue ran out of the door. Pranav, in his second month as an office assistant, was sorting forms when a woman in jeans, a faded band T-shirt and a nose ring walked straight to the counter. He barely looked up. "Madam, students queue outside, please. Form 3B is on the table." She smiled. "I'm not a student. I'm Dr. Usha Menon, the new head of chemistry. I need my staff ID." Pranav froze. The registrar behind him coughed. He had seen the clothes and filled in the rest: young, casual, must be a student. "I'm so sorry, ma'am. I assumed." "People often do," she said, unbothered. "Next time, maybe ask 'How can I help you?' first." He printed her ID with shaking hands. Later that week he caught himself sizing up a man in an expensive suit as a VIP donor, and asked instead. The man was a parent who'd lost his son's form.

qa.q: What did Dr. Usha Menon need?
qa.a: Her staff ID.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel after learning who she was?
qa.a: Pranav froze with embarrassment, hands shaking, realising he had judged her by her clothes.

qa.q: What habit did Pranav adopt after this?
qa.a: Asking 'How can I help you?' first instead of guessing someone's role from appearance, as he did with the man in the suit.

qa.q: How did Dr. Menon react to being mistaken for a student?
qa.a: She was unbothered, saying people often assume, and kindly suggested asking how to help first.

grounding: Shows a young worker guessing a person's role from clothes and accessories, being wrong twice over, and switching to asking.

passage:
Hi Bhupen,
You asked how the new flatmate is working out. Honestly, I got him completely wrong at first, and I'm a bit ashamed.
When Rizwan moved in, he had a long beard and a white cap, and he prayed on a mat in his room. Within about ten seconds I'd decided he'd be strict, would hate my music, and would judge me for everything. So I kept my door shut and my headphones on for two weeks.
Then one night my guitar amp broke, and he knocked on my door holding a screwdriver. Turns out he plays bass in a band in Bandra, knows more about amplifiers than I ever will, and had been too polite to ask me to jam. We fixed the amp at 1 am and played till the neighbours banged on the wall.
I built a whole person from a beard and a cap. Next time I'll just ask someone what they're into.
Eshaan

qa.q: Where does Rizwan's band play?
qa.a: In Bandra.

qa.q: How does Eshaan feel now about the first two weeks?
qa.a: Eshaan feels a bit ashamed of judging Rizwan from his beard and cap and of keeping the door shut.

qa.q: What does Eshaan plan to do next time?
qa.a: Simply ask people what they're into, with respectful curiosity, instead of drawing conclusions from appearance.

qa.q: How might Rizwan have experienced those two weeks?
qa.a: Rizwan may have felt a little shut out by the closed door and headphones, while being too polite to ask to play music together.

grounding: Shows a young adult guessing a flatmate's attitudes from religious dress, being wrong, and choosing curiosity over conclusions.

passage:
Okay, a confession for your podcast. My first week at the architecture firm, I made up a whole person out of an outfit. Hafsa sat opposite me: black headscarf, long sleeves, plain grey kurta, a very old phone. In my head, instantly: shy, strict family, probably not into after-work plans. So when the team went for karaoke on Friday, I didn't even ask her.
On Monday she said, very politely, "I heard karaoke was fun. Next time, can you tell me? I've been practising a song for months."
I wanted to disappear.
It turns out she grew up in Dubai, loves old Hindi film songs, and keeps the old phone because her late father gave it to her. Nothing I'd guessed was right. So now, when my brain starts writing someone's story from their clothes, I tell it: Maria, ask a question instead.

qa.q: Why does Hafsa keep the old phone?
qa.a: Because her late father gave it to her.

qa.q: How did Maria feel when Hafsa asked to be told next time?
qa.a: Maria felt deeply embarrassed and ashamed, wanting to disappear after leaving Hafsa out because of a guess.

qa.q: What does Maria do now when the guessing starts?
qa.a: Maria tells herself to ask a question instead of writing someone's story from their clothes.

qa.q: What was it like for Hafsa to be left out of karaoke?
qa.a: Hafsa was likely disappointed and a little hurt, having practised a song for months, though she raised it politely.

grounding: Guesses about someone's personality and background from clothes and accessories are often wrong and biased, so respectful curiosity is better than conclusions.
